Revealing mechanism of micro-aeration for enhancing volatile fatty acids 
production from swine manure 
Qitao Cao a,1, Wanqin Zhang a,1, Tianjing Lian a,b, Shunli Wang a, Fubin Yin a, Tanlong Zhou a, 
Xiaoman Wei a, Hongmin Dong a,* 
a Institute of Environment and Sustainable Development in Agriculture, Chinese Academy of Agricultural Sciences, Beijing 100081, PR China 
b College of Natural Resources and Environment, Northwest A&F University, Yangling 712100, PR China   
H I G H L I G H T  
G R A P H I C A L  A B S T R A C T

had 
significant 
improvement with VFAs increased by 
22.4%. 
• Air-micro-aeration at ORP +5.5 mV

A R T I C L E  I N F O   
Keywords: 
Bio-fermentation 
Micro-oxygen environment 
Agricultural waste 
Acid production 
Carbon mass balance 
Microbial communities 
A B S T R A C T   
Micro-aeration is considered a new strategy for improving volatile fatty acids (VFAs) production of agricultural 
waste. This study investigated the effect and mechanism of micro-aeration of air and oxygen (O2) on VFAs 
production from swine manure. The results showed that Air-micro-aeration had the most significant improve­
ment effect, with the highest VFAs of 8.21 g/L, which was increased by 22.4%. Moreover, the mixing effects of 
different micro-aeration were limited, and the microbial communities significantly varied. Firmicutes and Bac­
teroidota were the dominant hydrolytic and acidogenic bacteria, and Air-micro-aeration preferentially promoted 
electron transfer activity and energy generation. Methanosarcina, Methanocorpusculum, and Methanobrevibacter 
can adapt to environmental changes according to their different oxygen tolerance, and the consumption and 
conversion of VFAs by methanogens were slow under Air-micro-aeration condition. This study revealed mech­
anism of micro-aeration for improving VFAs production from swine manure, providing a theoretical basis for 
micro-aeration regulation optimization.

1. Introduction 
Micro-aerobic environment is a state between aerobic and anaerobic 
conditions with a low dissolved oxygen (DO) concentration, that is 
created by injecting a trace amount of air or oxygen (O2) (DO range of 
0.1-1.0 mg/L) into an anaerobic bioreactor (Wu et al., 2015; Chen et al., 
2020; Zhang et al., 2021). Recent studies have shown that micro- 
aeration is an effective approach that facilitates anaerobic digestion 
(AD), such as improving hydrolysis rate and enhancing methane pro­
duction (Nguyen and Khanal, 2018; Wang et al., 2020). The hydrolysis 
stage is generally regarded as a rate-limiting step of AD, especially when 
recalcitrant lignocellulosic biomass, such as straw, are used, and hy­
drolysis rates under aerobic and anoxic conditions are significantly 
higher than those under anaerobic conditions (Shrestha et al., 2017; 
Wang et al., 2020). 
Given that AD system has a certain tolerance to O2, micro-aeration 
can have a positive impact on microbial metabolism and energy trans­
fer. Lim et al. (2014) studied the co-digestion characteristics of brown 
water and food waste at a micro-aeration intensity of 5 and 7 mL O2 
L−1d−1, and the results showed that micro-aeration enhanced microbial 
diversity and volatile fatty acids (VFAs) production, and the hydrolysis 
rate and methane yield also increased. Microbial analysis indicated that 
micro-aeration can promote the proliferation of diverse bacterial pop­
ulations and increase the proportion of Firmicutes clones related to hy­
drolysis in contrast to anaerobic conditions (Lim et al., 2014). Yu et al. 
(2020) found that hydrolytic/fermentative bacteria and acetoclastic 
methanogens (e.g., Methanosaeta) were in higher abundances with 
controlled micro-aeration (5 and 10 mg O2/L-reactor), which facilitated 
syntrophic interactions between microorganisms. The relative abun­
dance of dominant bacterium Firmicutes increased from 58% to 72%, 
and the relative abundance of methanogenic archaea Methanosarcina 
and Methanobacterium with certain oxygen tolerance also increased (Fu 
et al., 2016). 
VFAs are the intermediate products and can be consumed at the 
methanogenic stage in AD. When air or O2 is introduced into an 
anaerobic reactor, the proliferation of strictly anaerobic methanogens is 
inhibited to a certain extent due to the enhanced activity of facultative 
hydrolysis bacteria and fermentation bacteria, and thus VFAs may 
accumulate. Lim and Wang et al. (2013) reported that VFAs concen­
tration increased from 1.69 g COD/L to 5.57 g COD/L after 4 days of 
micro-aeration pretreatment, and methane production increased by 
21%, but long-term experiment is needed to verify. It was reported in a 
previous study that the rate of methane production increased by 19.6%, 
through the mass-transfer (relative contributions of 62.9%) and micro- 
aerobic environment (relative contributions of 37.1%) (Yang and 
Deng, 2020). To prevent excessive VFAs accumulation under high OLR 
conditions, Nguyen et al. (2019) found that VFAs concentrations 
decreased from 9.84 g COD/L to 3.21 g COD/L at -470 mV after con­
ducting intermittent ORP-based micro-aeration control. To date, most 
studies on micro-aeration in AD aimed at improving methane produc­
tion. In the high-rate production of short chain carboxylic acids (SCCAs, 
including VFAs and lactic acid), Cao et al. (2022) confirmed that micro- 
aeration enhanced VFAs by 20.3% and shortened the time to reach the 
maximum from 18 days to 10 days, but the effect of micro-aeration on 
VFAs production requires more studies. The mechanism of micro- 
aeration promoting the production of VFAs still remains unclear. The 
reasons could be that micro-aerobic environment enhances metabolic 
activities of hydrolytic bacteria and acid-producing bacteria, or the gas 
mixing improves the mass transfer of organic matters. 
In this study, the effect and mechanism of micro-aeration on VFAs 
production were explored by comparing different micro-aeration (Air 
and O2) with N2 addition. It is expected to provide a theoretical basis for 
the optimization of VFAs production parameters and process improve­
ment of subsequent micro-aeration regulation, and a novel strategy for 
realizing an environment-friendly, economic and efficient acid produc­
tion process. 
Materials and methods 
1.1. Feedstock and inoculum 
Swine manure was collected from a pig farm in Changping, Beijing, 
and stored in a freezer at -20 ◦C before the use. The anaerobically 
digested sludge as inoculum was collected from an anaerobic reactor 
stably operated for a long time in the laboratory with a previously 
described method and heat-treated at 85 ◦C for 3 h (Cao et al., 2021). 
The physicochemical properties of swine manure and inoculum are 
shown in Table 1. N2 (purity ≥99.9%) and O2 (purity ≥99.2%) gases 
were purchased from Jinggao Gas Co., Ltd (Beijing). Room air 
(N2:79.7%, O2:20.2%, CO2:0.1%) was directly used for the micro- 
aeration of air source. 
1.2. Experimental design 
Experiments were performed using four sets of 6.5 L stainless steel 
batch reactors with effective volumes of 6.0 L. The reactor was equipped 
with pH, ORP, DO, and temperature sensors. For sample collection and 
testing of fermentation broth characteristics, the upper, middle, and 
lower sampling ports were set at different heights (10, 20 and 30 cm) 
above the bottom of the reactors. A 10 L gas collection bag was attached 
to the reactor for gas collection. The schematic diagram of micro- 
aeration-based AD system is shown in Supplementary Material. In this 
study, swine manure as the sole substrate was added to each reactor with 
a VS concentration of 4% and a substrate/inoculum ratio (v/v) of 9:1. 
The initial pH was adjusted to 10.0±0.2 by using 6.0 M NaOH, and the 
temperature was maintained at 35±1 ◦C by the outer wall of the reactor 
with a circulating water bath according to previous studies (Zhang et al., 
2020). A micro-aeration intensity of 1000 mL/L/d was conducted as 
previously described (Cao et al., 2022) and the micro-aeration sources 
were air and O2. ORP and pH changes during the experiment are shown 
in Supplementary Material. The experimental period was 24 days, and 
about 5 mL of liquid samples were collected from each reactor every 2 
days for analysis of characteristics. 
1.3. Analytical methods 
Total solids (TS) and volatile solids (VS) of swine manure and inoc­
ulum were measured according to the standard methods (APHA, 2005). 
C and N contents were determined with an elemental analyzer (Perkin 
Elmer 2400 SeriesII, Sheffied, UK). pH and ORP were measured with a 
pH meter (Easyferm Plus PHI S8 120, Hamilton, Switzerland) and an 
ORP meter (Oxytrode Platinum, Hamilton, Switzerland), respectively. 
Crude fiber was analyzed using a cellulose analyzer (ANKOM 220i, USA) 
following the Van Soest method (Soest, 1963). The volume and 
composition of the biogas were determined with a mass flow controller 
(ACU10FD-LC, ACCU, Beijing) and a portable biogas analyzer (Biogas 
5000, Geotech, UK). VFAs were analyzed as described by Cao et al. 
(2021).

To analyze the structure of microbial communities, approximately 5 
mL of samples were obtained from each reactor every 6 days. High- 
throughput sequencing was performed by Allwegene Technology Co. 
Ltd (Beijing, China) using an Illumina MiSeq platform (Illumina Lnc., 
CA, USA). The primer pairs 338F-806R and 344F-806R were used to 
amplify bacterial 16S rRNA and archaeal 16S rRNA genes, allowing the 
original sequence data to be generated. The functional characteristics of 
the microbial communities were analyzed by phylogenetic investigation 
of communities by reconstruction of unobserved states (PICRUSt), and 
the metabolic pathways were classified and generated based on the 
Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) database.

1.4. Data processing and statistical analysis 
All data were calculated using Microsoft Office Excel 2019. Data 
statistical analysis was performed using IBM SPSS Statistics 25, and the 
significance level was 0.05. All figures in this study were plotted using 
Origin 2021. 
2. Result and discussion 
2.1. Total Volatile fatty acids concentration changes under different 
micro-aeration conditions 
Changes in TVFAs concentration under different micro-aeration 
conditions were shown in Fig. 1A. According to the variation in TVFAs 
concentration under the Air-micro-aeration condition, the 24-day AD 
process was divided into three phases: Phase I: In the first 8 days, the 
concentration of TVFAs gradually accumulated; Phase II: From day 8 to 
day 18, the concentration of TVFAs remained stable; Phase III: After day 
18, the AD system entered the methanogenic stage, and the concentra­
tion of TVFAs decreased rapidly. 
In Phase I, the concentration of TVFAs demonstrated an upward 
trend under different micro-aeration conditions. The highest concen­
tration of TVFAs was achieved through Air-micro-aeration, and the 
maximum value was 8.21 g/L. Under N2 addition condition, the TVFAs 
concentration reached a maximum value (7.36 g/L) on day 4, and then 
remained stable at about 7.00 g/L. The highest TVFAs concentration by 
O2-micro-aeration was 6.62 g/L. For the improvement of TVFAs pro­
duction, O2-micro-aeration was lower than that of Air-micro-aeration 
and N2 addition, but higher than that of without micro-aeration. 
Compared with AD, Air-micro-aeration, N2 addition, and O2-micro- 
aeration improved TVFAs production by 22.4%, 17.8%, and 10.8%, 
respectively. In Phase II, Air-micro-aeration reactor maintained a stable 
acidification stage, with the highest and average TVFAs of 8.59 and 7.93 
g/L, respectively. However, the biogas of N2 addition and O2-micro- 
aeration reactors gradually increased (See Supplementary Material), 
and the average TVFAs dropped to 2.73 and 4.41 g/L, respectively. N2 
addition enhances the mass transfer of substrate and fosters the growth 
and activities of methanogens (Wang et al., 2020). Therefore, more VFAs 
(mainly acetic acid) were converted to CH4 (See Supplementary Mate­
rial) to make the VFA production relatively lower. Under anaerobic 
condition, TVFAs accumulated continuously, and the maximum con­
centration was 7.58 g/L. In Phase II, given that N2 addition and O2- 
micro-aeration reactors were still at the methanogenic stage, TVFAs 
continued to decrease. Air-micro-aeration reactor began to enter the 
methanogenic stage, and TVFAs decreased rapidly. The TVFAs of the 
anaerobic reactor had a maximum of 8.43 g/L on day 20, but the con­
centration began to decrease due to the AD system entered the meth­
anogenic stage. 
ORP is commonly used to measure the oxidative (more positive 
values) or reductive (more negative values) environment in an aqueous 
phase, and Nguyen et al. (2019) developed an ORP-controlled inter­
mittent micro-aeration system to improve the methane yield (ORP at 
+25 mV from the baseline ORP). In this study, compared with anaerobic 
conditions, N2 addition, Air-, and O2-micro-aeration increased ORP by 
about 1.5, 5.5, and 11.0 mV, respectively. O2-micro-aeration and Air- 
micro-aeration had a more significant improvement in ORP than N2 
addition. The relationship between relative ORP and TVFAs were shown 
in Fig. 2A. It was observed that Air-micro-aeration at an ORP +5.5 mV 
higher than the anaerobic ORP was favorable to TVFAs, especially acetic 
acid production, while O2-micro-aeration at an ORP +11.0 mV higher 
than the anaerobic ORP caused a significant reduction of TVFAs due to 
excess aerobic respiration. The same phenomenon was also observed in 
the AD of blackwater by micro-aeration, and the results indicated that 
the TVFAs increased from 90-269 mg/L to 339-396 mg/L with the ox­
ygen dosage increased from 0 (ORP=-308 mV) to 50 mg/g CODfeed 
(ORP=-109 mV), while the TVFAs decreased to 203-304 mg/L with the 
oxygen dosage continued to expand to 150 mg/g CODfeed (ORP=-69 
mV) (Guo et al.,2021). Intermittent micro-aeration at an ORP +25 mV 
higher than the baseline ORP accelerated the VFAs conversion rapidly, 
while when ORP +50 mV caused significant accumulation of VFA due to 
inhibition of methanogens as indicated by reduced methane yields 
(Nguyen et al., 2019). 
2.2. Total Volatile fatty acids composition distribution under different 
micro-aeration conditions 
As shown in Fig. 1B, acetic acid was the main component of VFAs, 
followed by propionic acid under different micro-aeration conditions in 
Phase I. Under the conditions of no micro-aeration (CK), Air-micro- 
aeration, N2 addition and O2-micro-aeration, the proportions of acetic 
acid at the maximum VFAs concentration were 62.7%, 61.8%, 56.9%, 
and 61.5%, respectively, and the proportions of propionic acid were 
19.0%, 23.4%, 25.3%, and 25.1%, respectively (Fig. 1B). The result 
showed that micro-aeration had no significant effect on TVFAs compo­
sition distribution in the early stage (P > 0.05). 
From day 8 to day 18, the TVFAs composition distribution under no 
micro-aeration, Air-micro-aeration and O2-micro-aeration conditions 
was similar to that in the first 8 days. However, under N2 addition

condition, the proportion of acetic acid was only 19.1%, and the pro­
portion of propionic acid increased to 75.5% at the peak of TVFA pro­
duction (Fig. 1B). The reason was that the AD system rapidly reached the 
methanogenic stage under N2 addition condition. 
After day 18, the percentages of acetic acid and propionic acid were 
64.1% and 19.9% (Fig. 1B), respectively, and no significant change in 
TVFAs components was found in the whole AD process without micro- 
aeration (P>0.05). Due to Air-micro-aeration reactor began to enter 
the methanogenic stage, acetic acid was rapidly converted into biogas, 
and the concentration decreased from 5.65 g/L (61.3%) to 3.20 g/L 
(47.7%). Compared with acetic acid, propionic acid was not easily 
converted into methane, and remained stable in Phases II and III, and its 
concentrations were 2.14 and 2.20 g/L, respectively. However, owing to 
a decrease in acetic acid content, the proportion of propionic acid 
increased from 23.2% to 31.1%. Methane production in the N2 addition 
reactor was nearly completed and the concentrations of acetic and 
propionic acid were only 0.22 (60.3%) and 0.15 g/L (39.7%), 
respectively. 
The results indicated that micro-aeration did not change the TVFAs 
composition distribution, and acetic acid was the main component. The 
TVFAs composition distribution is mainly related to the bacterial com­
munity. There was no significant change in the bacterial community (see 
Supplementary Material), and Firmicutes and Bacteroidota were the 
dominant hydrolysis and acidogenic bacteria under different micro- 
aeration conditions. 
2.3. Carbon mass balance at the peak of volatile fatty acids production 
The results of carbon mass balance at the peak of VFAs production 
under different micro-aeration conditions are shown in Fig. 2B. The 
carbon content in the residue was 68.6% without micro-aeration, and 
the hydrolysis rate was lower than the hydrolysis rates under micro- 
aeration conditions. Wang et al. (2020) investigated the effects of 
different nanobubble water (NBW) on the AD of cellulose for methane 
production, and the results showed that the rate of total organic carbon 
removal reached 31.8%, 34.1%, 34.6%, and 34.9% in deionized water, 
Air-NBW, N2-NBW, and O2-NBW, respectively, indicating that NBW 
enhanced cellulose hydrolysis. In the present study, given that no biogas 
production was observed in the anaerobic reactor (CK) before the VFAs 
reached the maximum, most of the soluble organic carbon (82.8%) was 
retained in the form of VFAs. Different from other reactors, the Air- 
micro-aeration reactor involved exogenous carbon due to the intro­
duced CO2, which may be a factor that should be considered in calcu­
lating carbon mass balance. Until the VFAs reached the maximum levels 
in the Air-micro-aeration reactor (Day 14), the carbon content of 
introduced CO2 was only 0.07 g, whereas the carbon content of the 
substrate was about 94.32 g. In terms of accumulated biogas, the carbon 
content in the form of CH4 and CO2 was 1.17 and 6.82 g, respectively, 
and thus exogenous carbon that entered the reactor through Air-micro- 
aeration was not considered. The highest hydrolysis rate was obtained 
under the Air-micro-aeration condition and increased by 15.3% relative 
to that in No-micro-aeration. The carbon content of the hydrolysate was 
63.6% for VFAs production, 20.2% for biogas, including CH4 and CO2, 
and 16.2% for other forms. N2 addition and O2-micro-aeration did not 
improve the hydrolysis rate of fermentation materials, but the maximum 
VFAs level was lower than that under Air-micro-aeration or anaerobic 
condition. The results showed that the hydrolyzed organic carbon was 
not effectively transformed into VFAs and converted into biogas and 
other soluble substances (proteins, polysaccharides, amino acids, 
structural components of cells, etc.), especially microbial biomass. The 
carbon content in other forms under N2 addition and O2-micro-aeration 
conditions was 10.9% and 14.6%, respectively. In this study, the same 
amount of O2 gas and air were injected into the reactors daily and the 
reactor with O2 gas received approximately four times more oxygen than 
that with air gas, since air contained about 21% oxygen gas. So, O2- 
micro-aeration has a higher aeration intensity than Air-micro-aeration. 
A high aeration intensity is favorable for microbial growth, and the 
total soluble hydrolysate used for biomass generation is as high as 
18.5%, which is only 0.9% and 6.6% under anaerobic and appropriate 
micro-aeration conditions, respectively (Xu et al., 2014). Electron 
transport system activities (ETS) generally occurs in the bacterial cell 
membrane (Szabo, 2003). The highest ETS activity of O2-NBW, N2-NBW 
and Air-NBW reactors increased by 1.7, 1.6 and 1.1 times compared to 
the control (Wang et al., 2020). ETS can transfer electrons from the 
coenzymes (NADH, NADPH) produced by the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) 
cycle to the terminal electron acceptor in the oxidative phosphorylation 
(electron transport) pathway. The surface of NBs has negative charges 
and can attract NAD+ (Kyzas et al., 2019); NBs also have a higher 
movement speed, favoring the movement of NAD+, which is used for the 
reduction reaction to generate NADH. Therefore, although N2 addition 
and O2-micro-aeration increased substrate degradation, it was a carbon 
loss for VFAs production due to the hydrolysate was not conducive to 
VFAs accumulation. 
2.4. Microbial community analysis 
2.4.1. Bacterial phyla 
The observed_species index represents the number of OTUs actually 
observed as sequencing depth increases. Under the Air-micro-aeration, 
N2 addition and O2-micro-aeration conditions, the observed_species 
index increased gradually and then decreased after reaching the peak 
(Fig. 3). N2 addition and O2-micro-aeration increased the number of 
bacteria rapidly, which reached its peak on day 6. The observed_species 
index under Air-micro-aeration and anaerobic conditions increased 
slowly, but the peaks were higher than those under N2 addition and O2- 
micro-aeration conditions. The observed_species index was positively 
correlated with VFAs production (P < 0.05), indicating that the increase 
in bacterial number was beneficial to VFAs production. 
There was no significant change in the bacterial community struc­
tures at the class level under different micro-aeration conditions (see 
supplementary material). The dominant bacterial communities were 
Clostridia and Bacilli (Fig. 4A), respectively, and the sum of their relative 
abundance accounted for about 80% throughout the experiment. Clos­
tridia and Bacilli belong to Firmicutes, which can produce extracellular 
enzymes (such as cellulases, lipases, and proteases) that play key roles in 
the metabolism of lignocellulose, proteins and lipids (Lim et al., 2014). 
Clostridia belongs to anaerobic gram-positive bacteria, most of which 
can convert various carbon sources, including complex lignocellulose, 
into VFAs (mainly acetate and butyrate), propanol, and butanol (Chai 
et al., 2019b; Diallo et al., 2021). Bacilli widely exist in compost and soil 
and degrade lignocellulose and protein to produce butyrate (Zalma and 
El-Sharoud, 2021). Bacilli and Bacteroidia possess the buk pathway, 
while Clostridia can produce butyrate via both the buk and but pathways 
(Chai et al., 2019a). In addition, Bacteroidia utilize anaerobic respiration 
for glycolysis to produce acetate and isovalerate (Joyce et al., 2018). It is 
one of the classes of anaerobic bacteria with the highest resistance to 
oxygen, maintaining a high relative abundance during the whole AD 
process of this study. 
2.4.2. Archaeal genus 
As shown in Fig. 4C, Methanosarcina and Methanobrevibacter were the 
dominant archaeal genus at the beginning, accounting for 66% and 31%, 
respectively. After micro-aeration, the archaeal community structure at 
the genus level significantly varied. Under anaerobic condition, Meth­
anosarcina became the dominant genus, with a relative abundance of 
77%. Methanosarcina has the ability to use both acetate and CO2/H2 to 
produce methane (De Vrieze et al., 2012). The abundance of Meth­
anosarcina decreased to 32% after Air-micro-aeration, and Meth­
anocorpusculum increased to become the dominant genus, with a relative 
abundance of 37%. Under N2 addition condition, the relative abundance 
of Methanosarcina was as high as 96%. However, the relative abundance 
of Methanosarcina decreased significantly to 17% through O2-micro-

aeration, and the relative abundance of Methanobrevibacter and Meth­
anocorpusculum increased to 45% and 23%, respectively. Methano­
brevibacter (Leadbetter and Breznak, 1996) and Methanocorpusculum 
(Gilmore et al., 2017) are strictly hydrogenotrophic methanogens (CH4 
production via CO2/H2). Nguyen et al. (2019) also observed a similar 
phenomenon that the shift of dominant archaeal genus from Meth­
anosarcina to Methanobrevibacter and Methanocorpusculum have occurred 
during ORP-based micro-aeration. Methanocorpusculum showed certain 
oxygen tolerance, was able to adapt to an aerobic environment, and 
maintained a high relative abundance. Methanobrevibacter showed 
strong oxygen tolerance and became the dominant bacterium with the 
highest relative abundance under O2-micro-aeration condition. These 
results implied that the oxygen tolerance of Methanosarcina, Meth­
anocorpusculum, and Methanobrevibacter increased in turn. 
2.5. Preliminary analysis on regulation mechanisms 
Three sampling ports were set at different heights (10, 20 and 30 cm) 
above the base of the reactor for TS analysis. The TS concentration of the 
fermentation broth in the reactor was measured before and after micro- 
aeration. The mixing degree of the fermentation broth was assessed 
according to the coefficient of variation (CV) of TS concentration (Yang 
and Deng, 2020) and the results are shown in Fig. 5. In order to explore 
the mixing effect of micro-aeration, the mechanical stirring in the re­
actors was not started during the whole AD process. Many solids settled 
in the lower layers of the reactors, resulting in a large CV value of about 
0.55. The CV values all decreased in different micro-aeration processes, 
and a minimum of about 0.20 was obtained by N2 addition. The mini­
mum CV value of Air-micro-aeration was about 0.45, which was slightly 
lower than that of O2-micro-aeration. Different micro-aeration processes 
with same intensity had different effects on the degree of mixing 
possibly due to difference in solubility among different gas sources in 
water. Under normal temperature and pressure, the volume solubility of 
N2, Air and O2 in water are 0.016, 0.019, and 0.031, respectively. N2 has 
the lowest solubility in water and cannot be utilized by microorganisms, 
and thus N2 addition had the greatest impact on the degree of mixing. 
Compared with N2, O2 has higher solubility in water and can be 
consumed and utilized by facultative bacteria or removed by reducing 
substances in reactors. Therefore, O2-micro-aeration had the least 
impact on the degree of mixing. 
Although the solubility of air in water was similar to that of N2 and 
lower than that of O2 in water, the components in air (mainly O2 and 
CO2) can be consumed and utilized by microorganisms. Thus, the in­
fluence on the degree of mixing was less than that of N2. Gas solubility 
might not be the major reason for the difference in mixing degree, 
indicated by the similar mixing degree for air and O2 (Fig. 5). Other 
reasons impacting the mixing degree possibly lie in the consumption and 
utilization rate of gas components (especially O2) by microorganisms. In 
addition, due to the different physicochemical properties, different gas 
types can generate different bubble stabilities and structures at the 
gas–liquid interface (Zhang et al., 2021). For example, the bubble sta­
bility of different gases followed the order H2>air>N2>CO2 (Wang 
et al., 2019). After micro-aeration was stopped, the solid components in 
the reactor gradually settled, and the CV value of TS concentration 
increased. At 120 min, the CV value in different micro-aeration reactors 
returned to the same level. Among these micro-aeration methods, N2 
addition had the greatest impact on the degree of mixing. However, 
compared with the definition of uniform mixing in Yang et al. (2021) 
and Wu (2012), the CV value was less than 0.02 or 0.05. In this study, 
the minimum CV value (about 0.20) was achieved by N2 addition, which 
was much greater than the CV value of uniform mixing. Therefore, the 
mixing effect of micro-aeration in this study was limited, and the reason 
for the difference in the mixing effect of different micro-aeration re­
actors was mainly caused by the nature of the gas source itself. Different 
from this study, Yang and Deng (2020) reported that air and biogas 
mixing modes achieved the same mixing efficiency and all improved the 
mass transfer effect when the aeration intensity was calculated accord­
ing to the same power input of mechanical mixing. Therefore, when the 
contribution of improved mass transfer and the reaction of microaerobic 
environment to methane production were considered, the different 
mixing effects of the gas source were ignored due to the high aeration 
intensity. In fact, the mixing effect of micro-aeration is related to the 
aeration rate or intensity.

ance due to several mechanisms. On the one hand, facultative bacteria 
with rapid oxygen consumption capacities can consume dissolved

other hand, some methanogens have a certain level of oxygen tolerance, 
but the oxygen tolerance of different methanogens varies (Brioukhanov 
et al., 2006; Horne and Lessner, 2013; Angle et al., 2017). Meth­
anosarcina and Methanobrevibacter are known to produce anti-oxidative 
enzymes (such as superoxide dismutase (SOD), catalase, and peroxi­

and exhibit high oxygen tolerance (Nguyen and Khanal, 2018). Fu et al. 
(2016) investigated the impact of micro-aeration on microbial com­
munity structure, and the relative abundance of oxytolerant Meth­
anosarcina and Methanobacterium doubled in the micro-aerobic 
environment compared with that under anaerobic condition. In the 
present study, Methanosarcina, Methanocorpusculum, and Methano­
brevibacter exhibited different levels of oxygen tolerance, and 
methanogenic archaea showed survival mechanisms that can adapt to 
changes in oxygen levels in the environment by adjusting their com­
munity structures according to different levels of oxygen tolerance. 
The metabolic functions based on the KEGG pathway databases 
exhibited differences among different micro-aeration conditions, 
although the magnitude of difference was relatively low (Fig. 6). Genes 
related to glycolysis/gluconeogenesis, the citrate cycle (i.e., TCA cycle), 
pentose phosphate pathway, and purine metabolism, which are directly 
related to the efficiency of hydrolysis and acidification, were more 
abundant under the Air-micro-aeration condition (Zhang et al., 2022). 
Air or oxygen bubbles with negative charges promote nicotinamide 
adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) transfer, thereby increasing the produc­
tion of the reduced form nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NADH) 
(Kyzas et al., 2019). Therefore, redox balance can be maintained by 
regenerating NADH from fermentation intermediates, such as VFAs, 
which produce small amounts of ATP (Zhang et al., 2021). A trace 
amount of oxygen was introduced into the anaerobic bioreactor as the 
terminal electron acceptor to accelerate the hydrolysis of complex 
organic matter by facultative bacteria and enhance the electron transfer

activity of microbial metabolism (Botheju et al., 2009). Reducing oxy­
gen with NADH can release a large amount of energy, which further 
generates a proton gradient to drive ATP synthesis and transport other 
metabolites and increase the efficiency of hydrolysis and acidification 
(Kyzas et al., 2019). In addition, some facultative and aerobic micro­
organisms can use trace oxygen to completely oxidize acetyl-CoA into 
CO2 through aerobic metabolism, such as the TCA cycle (Nguyen and 
Khanal, 2018). VFAs are not only the products of microbial decompo­
sition of macromolecular organics, but can also be utilized by microbial 
respiration and metabolism. The VFAs concentration detected in 
fermentation broth is actually the result of the balance between pro­
duction and consumption. In general, the abundance of functional genes 
can reflect the biomass of functional microorganisms in the system. As 
shown in Fig 6, the high abundance of functional genes can indicate the 
strong metabolic activity of microorganisms, but it also means that there 
is a large demand for VFAs as a carbon source. Under O2-micro-aeration 
condition, VFAs can be more rapidly consumed for microbial growth and 
aerobic respiration (Xu et al., 2014), resulting in an increased CO2 
content in biogas considerably (see Supplementary Material). 
3. Challenges and perspectives 
In recent years, micro-aeration has been investigated as an effective 
approach to facilitate the performance of AD process and involves 
controlling VFAs accumulation, stabilizing the process, scavenging H2S, 
improving VFAs production, and enhancing hydrolysis and overall 
methane yield (Nguyen and Khanal, 2018; Chen et al., 2020; Zhang 
et al., 2021). In this study, the regulation mechanism of micro-aeration 
for VFAs production was revealed through the comparison of the three 
gas sources of micro-aeration. In fact, the influence of micro-aeration on 
the efficiency and performance of VFAs production is related to two 
aspects: oxygen transfer rate (OTR) and oxygen utilization rate (OUR). 
The OTR in micro-aeration AD mainly depends on micro-aeration rate, 
aeration method, reactor configuration, and TS content of substrate 
(Garcia-Ochoa and Gomez, 2009), and the OUR depends on substrate 
(type and loading rate) and inoculum used (microbial community) (Díaz 
et al., 2011; Lim and Wang, 2013; Sawatdeenarunat et al., 2017; Xu 
et al., 2014). However, OTR and OUR under micro-aerobic conditions 
with different reactor configurations and operating conditions have yet 
to be established. In addition, precise automatic online data acquisition 
and supervisory control systems should be explored in future studies. 
More practical continuous and long-term experiments with different 
organic loading rates are needed to further verify the research results. 
Research on microbial composition and the behavior of microor­
ganisms are helpful in gaining deeper insights into the activity and 
biochemical pathways of micro-aeration-based AD for VFAs production 
and large-scale applications. However, such information is still limited. 
State-of-the-art techniques, such as meta-omic analyses and stable 
isotope labeling, should be used in further revealing the microbial 
community structures, microbial kinetics, genes expression, and meta­
bolic pathways under micro-aeration condition. Future research will be 
conducted to detect the genes of terminal electron transfer for under­
lying the mechanism in-depth. For example, fabG is associated with the 
coding of acyl reductases that use NAD+ or NADP+ as electron acceptor 
in lipid metabolism and fatty acid synthesis (Zhang et al., 2017); DesA3 
is related to acyl reductase, which acts on paired donors to bind or 
reduce molecular oxygen directly involved in fatty acid formation 
(Kachroo et al., 2006). 
4. Conclusions 
This study revealed the regulation mechanism of micro-aeration for 
VFAs production from swine manure. VFAs production improved in the 
first 8 days, and the maximum increased by 22.4% through Air-micro- 
aeration. Air-micro-aeration at an ORP +5.5 mV higher than the 
anaerobic ORP was favorable to TVFAs production, while O2-micro- 
aeration at an ORP +11.0 mV higher than the anaerobic ORP caused 
TVFAs reduction due to excess aerobic respiration. The mixing effects of 
different micro-aeration were limited and no significant change in the 
bacterial community. Air-micro-aeration enhanced electron transfer 
activity and microbial metabolism. Archaeal community structure can 
adjust according to oxygen tolerance.
